summary:
Rwanda does not criminalise same-sex intimacy. The age of consent is 18 regardless of sexual orientation or gender, and no statute criminalises transgender identity or consensual relationships as such.

Rwandan law forbids changing legal gender, so no legal gender recognition path exists and a trans visitor's documents cannot be aligned with lived gender under local law. Identity checks are where that absence becomes an enforcement encounter: the Human Rights First Rwanda Association's 2025 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents law-enforcement abuse directed at transgender people, including harassment during identity checks and arbitrary arrests on vagrancy and public-order grounds.

Violent detentions of transgender people in Rwanda were reported by Vice on 20 November 2020. On 25 December 2018, Bella, a singer booked to perform at a hotel in Kigali, was stopped by police officers on the street after her show; her name was changed over concerns for her safety. A 2016 U.S. State Department report recorded LGBT Rwandans being harassed, blackmailed and arrested by police under public-order and morality laws, together with reports from LGBTI rights groups of harassment by neighbours and police during that period.

Constitutional Article 26 recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman, so same-sex marriages, civil unions and similar unions are not recognised. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore has no recognised partnership status in Rwanda.

No general anti-discrimination protection covers gender identity. Constitutional Articles 15 and 16 do not bar discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and Article 16's list of protected grounds omits both, leaving a trans visitor without a domestic non-discrimination claim.

Protection machinery is set out in standing instructions. The 2024 asylum and humanitarian protection Standard Operating Procedures require interviews to be conducted so the individual can present the grounds of their application comprehensively, with trained interviewers taking account of gender and any circumstance including sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability. The 2014 Refugee Appeal Tribunal Standard Operating Procedures require hearings to take account of the appellant's sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability. The 2024 Standard Operating Procedures on identifying and safeguarding vulnerable persons under the Migration and Economic Development Partnership define Vulnerable Persons to include individuals whose gender identity and/or sexual orientation place them at higher risk, expressly naming transgender persons. A transgender claimant was granted refugee status in April 2022, and in 2024 the government issued immigration and asylum protections covering LGBTQ people.

Access to organised support is constrained. LGBTIQ organisations cannot register openly, and NGO Law No. 058/2024, adopted in June 2024, has raised freedom-of-association concerns. A public Pride event was held in 2021.
tangentialFactors:
Official posture on the question has been framed as non-engagement. Asked about LGBT life in Rwanda at a cultural event abroad on 25 September 2016, President Paul Kagame replied that 'it hasn't been our problem. And we don't intend to make it our problem'.

Homosexuality is described as a taboo topic in Rwanda with no significant public discussion, and LGBTQ people face stigmatisation among the broader population. In September 2019, gospel singer Albert Nabonibo came out as gay on a Christian YouTube channel, prompting shock and hostile reactions from family and friends, while the Minister of State for East African Community Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe, publicly backed him.

The Anglican Church of Rwanda condemned non-biblical behaviours of Western churches in 2007 and refused to support the ordination of LGBTQ clergy.

The Outright International Rwanda overview, dated 12 March 2026, is the most recently updated source underlying the assessment above.
localsOnly:
The Patients Rights and Responsibilities Policy, issued by the Rwandan Ministry of Health in 2018, states that all Rwandans, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, age, religion, cultural belief or disability, are equally entitled to receive health services to promote and maintain good health; it applies across public, private and NGO sectors.

Three internal instruments name sexual orientation as a protected ground without naming gender identity: the Human Resource Management Policy (2015) of the Office of the Auditor General of State Finances lists sexual orientation as a prohibited ground for harassment; the Code of Conduct of the Public Private Partnership Guidelines (2018) bans discrimination against bidders on grounds of sexual orientation; and Law 058/2021 on Protection of Personal Data and Privacy protects a person's sexual life as sensitive personal data.

The Horizons Community Association of Rwanda has conducted public advocacy for LGBTQ rights since 2005, and its members have often been harassed by the government.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific killing figure, count or rate appears in the sources, and no denominator or general homicide rate is provided, so no comparison between transgender violence and background violence can be drawn from this inventory.

The most recent dated incident of violence directed at transgender people in the sources is 20 November 2020. The 2025 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents abuse at identity checks and arbitrary arrests but supplies no dated individual cases, so no later specific incident is sourced here.

No youth-specific, minor-specific or education-specific findings appear in the sources: school policy, bullying and medication carriage by minors are not covered, and no youth-specific care access findings are present either.

Whether NGO Law No. 058/2024 has been applied against LGBTIQ organisations in practice is unresolved in this inventory; only the freedom-of-association concern raised at its adoption is sourced.

Whether document-marker mismatch or gender presentation triggers secondary screening at Rwandan entry points is not sourced; the inventory contains no airport or border-screening evidence for Rwanda.

The inventory's material on pre-colonial same-sex relations in the Great Lakes region and in the old Kingdom of Rwanda is historical and carries no trans-specific bearing, and the social-climate claims rest largely on a Wikipedia country page and a 2012 blog post.
